propositions.text: The 'due care' standard was introduced into the Patent Act in October 2019 to meet obligations under the Patent Law Treaty.
propositions.quote: The 'due care' standard was introduced into the Patent Act, RSC, 1985, c P-4 in October 2019 to satisfy obligations under the Patent Law Treaty.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph explains the 'due care' standard's introduction into the Patent Act in 2019 to comply with the Patent Law Treaty.

propositions.text: This is a judicial review of the December 20, 2022 decision of the Commissioner denying reinstatement of the patent.
propositions.quote: This is a judicial review of a December 20, 2022 decision of the Commissioner of Patents that denied the Applicant’s request for reinstatement of Canadian Patent No. 2,690,767.

propositions.text: The decision involved the deemed expiry of the patent for failure to pay maintenance fees.
propositions.quote: after it was deemed to have expired for failure to pay the tenth anniversary maintenance fee on the issued patent.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph states the judicial review concerns the Commissioner's denial of patent reinstatement after deemed expiry.

propositions.text: The Commissioner was not satisfied that the failure to pay occurred despite due care.
propositions.quote: The Commissioner was not satisfied that the failure to pay the maintenance fee by the prescribed due date occurred in spite of the due care required by the circumstances having been taken.

propositions.text: The Commissioner refused to reverse the deemed expiry of the patent.
propositions.quote: As such, the Commissioner refused to make the determination required to reverse the deemed expiry of the 767 Patent.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph reports the Commissioner's conclusion that due care was not demonstrated, leading to refusal to reinstate the patent.

propositions.text: The decision was reasonable and procedural fairness was maintained.
propositions.quote: I find the Decision was reasonable and that there was no breach of procedural fairness.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: As such, the application shall be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the decision was reasonable and dismisses the application.

propositions.text: Subsections 27.1(1) and 46(1) of the Patent Act require payment of maintenance fees to keep a patent in good standing.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to subsections 27.1(1) and 46(1) of the Patent Act, an applicant must pay annual maintenance fees to maintain a patent application and once it has issued its corresponding patent, in good standing.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph states statutory requirements for maintenance fee payments to keep a patent valid.

propositions.text: Failure to pay maintenance fees by the due date allows a six-month late fee period.
propositions.quote: If the prescribed maintenance fee for an issued patent is not paid by its due date, subsection 46(3) of the Patent Act provides a further time-period of six months.

propositions.text: Notice of potential deemed expiration must be provided if fees are unpaid after the late fee period.
propositions.quote: The Commissioner is required to provide notice of the potential for deemed expiration where the maintenance fee and late fee are not paid by the end of the late fee period.

propositions.text: Patent term deemed to expire if fees are unpaid after late fee period and two months after notice.
propositions.quote: The term of a patent will be deemed to expire where the maintenance fee and late fee have not been paid before the later of the late fee period and the end of two months after the date when the Commissioner provides notice.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph explains the process and timing for deemed patent expiry due to unpaid fees.

propositions.text: Reinstatement of a deemed-expired patent requires a request within 12 months, explanation, and payment of fees.
propositions.quote: A patent that has been deemed to expire may by reinstated if the requirements of subsection 46(5) of the Patent Act are satisfied.

propositions.text: Reinstatement requires showing failure occurred despite due care, within 12 months of late fee period.
propositions.quote: the patentee must request reversal of the deemed expiration within 12 months after the end of the late fee period, provide an explanation for why the maintenance fee was not paid, and pay all of the requisite fees.

propositions.text: The 'due care' standard is part of the reinstatement criteria, introduced by amendments to the Patent Act.
propositions.quote: In addition, the Commissioner must be satisfied that the failure to pay the maintenance fee 'occurred in spite of the due care required by the circumstances having been taken.' The requirement for the Commissioner to be satisfied that there has been due care arises from amendments to the Patent Act flowing from Canada joining the PLT.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph details the criteria and process for reinstating a deemed-expired patent, including due care.

propositions.text: The applicant and respondents are inventors and owners of the 767 Patent, a wide ice resurfacing machine.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, Robert Taillefer, and the Respondent, Sylvain Fredette, are named inventors and owners of the 767 Patent, titled 'Wide Ice Resurfacing Machine'.

propositions.text: The 767 Patent describes a machine capable of resurfacing a wider ice surface.
propositions.quote: The 767 Patent is a patent for an ice resurfacing machine that is described as having the capacity to resurface a wider surface area than traditional ice resurfacing machines.

propositions.text: Mr. Taillefer implemented the invention on the Rideau Canal surface.
propositions.quote: Mr. Taillefer is alleged to have implemented the invention claimed in the 767 Patent on the skating surface on the Rideau Canal.

propositions.text: The applicant's patent portfolio includes the 767 Patent.
propositions.quote: His patent portfolio consists of two patents, one of which is the 767 Patent.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph describes the patent's subject, ownership, and Mr. Taillefer's implementation of the invention.

propositions.text: The application for the 767 Patent was filed on January 21, 2010, and issued on January 19, 2016.
propositions.quote: The application for the 767 Patent was filed on January 21, 2010 and issued to patent on January 19, 2016.

propositions.text: The patent has been managed by a patent agency from the start.
propositions.quote: It has been managed from the outset by a patent agency firm appointed by the Applicant.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph states the filing and issuance dates and management of the patent.

propositions.text: Starting in 2012, the applicant was required to pay annual maintenance fees.
propositions.quote: Beginning in 2012, the Applicant was required to pay annual maintenance fees for the 767 application and then the 767 Patent.

propositions.text: The fees were due around January 20 each year.
propositions.quote: The maintenance fees were due on or about January 20th of each year.

propositions.text: The applicant's arrangement was to instruct the agent before payment.
propositions.quote: The arrangement between Mr. Taillefer and his Agent was that the Agent required instructions from Mr. Taillefer before paying the annual maintenance fee.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph explains the fee payment schedule and instructions process.

propositions.text: From 2010 to 2019, the applicant and agent communicated by email about maintenance fees.
propositions.quote: From 2010 to 2019, Mr. Taillefer and his Agent consistently communicated by email, including starting in 2012 with respect to payment of the annual maintenance fee.

propositions.text: Communication was through the same email address during this period.
propositions.quote: Communication was made with Mr. Taillefer through the same email address for the full time period.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph states consistent email communication between the applicant and agent.

propositions.text: In 2019, the agent sought instructions early for the 2020 fee, five months before the deadline.
propositions.quote: the Agent sought instructions for payment of the January 20, 2020 maintenance fee early, by sending correspondence to Mr. Taillefer’s email five months before the deadline.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph notes early fee instruction requests in 2019 for the 2020 fee.

propositions.text: Reminders were sent in December 2019, January 2020, indicating no payment without instructions.
propositions.quote: further reminders were sent to Mr. Taillefer by email on December 17, 2019, January 6, 2020 and January 20, 2020. The reminder emails indicated that the maintenance fee would not be paid without specific instructions to do so.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph describes reminder emails sent before the fee deadline, stating no payment without instructions.

propositions.text: The agent did not pay the fee because no instructions were received.
propositions.quote: As instructions were not received, the Agent did not pay the maintenance fee by January 20, 2020.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph states the fee was not paid due to lack of instructions.

propositions.text: In March 2020, the agent informed the applicant that the fee was unpaid and the late fee deadline was July 21, 2020.
propositions.quote: On March 31, 2020, the Agent sent email correspondence to Mr. Taillefer, advising that payment had not been made and that the deadline for correction through payment of a late fee was July 21, 2020.

propositions.text: Reminders were sent in July 2020.
propositions.quote: Two further communications were sent to Mr. Taillefer’s email as reminders on July 16, 2020 and July 17, 2020.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph reports notices of unpaid fee and late fee deadline, with reminders in July 2020.

propositions.text: In October 2020, the applicant was notified that the patent was deemed expired.
propositions.quote: On October 20, 2020, the Agent notified Mr. Taillefer by email of correspondence received from the Canadian Intellectual Property Office advising that the 767 Patent was deemed expired.

propositions.text: The applicant found the correspondence in his junk email folder and instructed the agent to seek reinstatement.
propositions.quote: On October 29, 2020, Mr. Taillefer found the correspondence in his junk email folder and instructed the Agent to seek reinstatement of the 767 Patent.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph describes the expiry notification and the applicant's response to seek reinstatement.

propositions.text: The agent filed a reinstatement request on November 16, 2020, with an explanation about the email issue.
propositions.quote: On November 16, 2020, the Agent filed a request to reinstate the 767 Patent under subsection 46(5) of the Patent Act, along with payment of the required fees.

propositions.text: The request included background about the email correspondence and the late discovery.
propositions.quote: Included in his request, the Agent provided background relating to the email correspondence sent to the Applicant regarding the outstanding fee payment and explained that the emails were only found in the Applicant’s junk folder on October 29, 2020.

propositions.text: The agent stated the applicant did not cause emails to go to junk and acted immediately after learning of expiry.
propositions.quote: The Agent indicated that '[t]o the best of his knowledge, the patent owner did not take any actions which would cause [the] emails to be directed to his junk folder, and had no reason to regularly check his junk folder for relevant emails.' The Agent highlighted that prior maintenance fees had always been paid ahead of the deadline and that the Applicant acted immediately upon learning that the 767 Patent was deemed expired.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph details the reinstatement request, including the explanation about email issues and prompt action.

propositions.text: In August 2021, the manager at CIPO advised the agent of an intention to refuse reinstatement.
propositions.quote: On August 3, 2021, the Manager of Patent Policy at CIPO, acting for and on behalf of the Commissioner, advised the Agent that the Commissioner intended to refuse the request to reinstate the 767 Patent.

propositions.text: The agent responded with a further response in August 2021.
propositions.quote: The Agent was invited to submit a response to the Preliminary Decision before a final decision was made, and submitted a further response on August 31, 2021.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph describes the preliminary refusal and the agent’s response.

propositions.text: The Commissioner refused the reinstatement request on December 20, 2022.
propositions.quote: On December 20, 2022, the Commissioner issued the Decision, refusing the Applicant’s request to reverse the deemed expiry of the 767 Patent.

propositions.text: The Commissioner was not satisfied that the failure to pay occurred despite due care.
propositions.quote: The Commissioner indicated that they were 'not satisfied that the failure to pay the prescribed fees on or before the due date occurred in spite of the due care required by the circumstances having been taken'.

propositions.text: The decision was based on the failure to meet the due care standard.
propositions.quote: and that the patentee had failed to meet the due care standard as enacted in paragraph 46(5)(b) of the Patent Act.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph states the final decision to refuse reinstatement, citing failure to demonstrate due care.

propositions.text: The Commissioner found a communication breakdown but did not find all measures were taken to avoid failure.
propositions.quote: While the Commissioner found that there was an unexpected breakdown in communication between the Applicant and Agent, they did not find that the Applicant had taken all measures that a reasonably prudent patent holder would have taken given the set of circumstances to avoid the failure, and for the failure to have occurred despite having taken those measures.

paragraphs.summary: The paragraph notes communication issues but concludes not all prudent measures were taken to prevent failure.

propositions.text: Two issues: whether the Decision was reasonable and if procedural fairness was breached.
propositions.quote: There are two broad issues raised by this application.

propositions.text: Standard of review for reasonableness and procedural fairness.
propositions.quote: Reasonableness is the presumptive standard of review of the merits of a decision...Questions of procedural fairness ask whether the procedure was fair.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies two issues: reasonableness of the decision and procedural fairness.

propositions.text: Reasonableness is the standard of review for merits, focusing on coherence, rationality, justification, transparency, and intelligibility.
propositions.quote: Reasonableness is the presumptive standard of review of the merits of a decision: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 23-25.

propositions.text: The court's role is to assess if the decision is justified, not to reweigh facts or substitute its judgment.
propositions.quote: which is not to conduct a de novo review of an administrative decision, or to determine whether they would have arrived at the same outcome.

propositions.text: A decision is reasonable if it is justified, transparent, and intelligible when read as a whole.
propositions.quote: it bears the hallmarks of justification, transparency, and intelligibility: Vavilov at paras 91-95, 99‑100.

paragraphs.summary: Reasonableness review assesses if the decision is coherent, justified, transparent, and intelligible, not reweighing facts or substituting judgment.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness asks if the procedure was fair, considering all circumstances, especially if the applicant knew the case and could respond.
propositions.quote: Questions of procedural fairness ask whether the procedure was fair having regard to all of the circumstances with the ultimate question being whether the applicant knew the case it had to meet and had a full and fair chance to respond.

propositions.text: The ultimate question is whether the applicant had a full and fair opportunity to respond to the case against them.
propositions.quote: the ultimate question being whether the applicant knew the case it had to meet and had a full and fair chance to respond.

paragraphs.summary: Procedural fairness considers whether the applicant was given a fair chance to respond, based on all circumstances.

propositions.text: The applicant challenges the standard of due care applied by the Commissioner, claiming it was both unreasonable and procedurally unfair.
propositions.quote: The Applicant takes issue with the standard of due care applied by the Commissioner.

propositions.text: The applicant argues the standard was higher than that communicated in the Manual of Patent Office Practice and was applied illogically.
propositions.quote: He asserts that the Decision is both objectively unreasonable as the Commissioner applied a standard of due care other than that of a reasonable patentee, and procedurally unfair as the Commissioner applied a different standard of due care than the standard communicated to the public.

propositions.text: The applicant claims the Commissioner’s reasoning was illogical, confusing, and prevented understanding of the case to meet.
propositions.quote: He further asserts that the delay in rendering the Decision was procedurally unfair.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant disputes the standard of due care applied, claiming it was higher than communicated and applied illogically, causing unfairness.

propositions.text: The Commissioner referred to the standard of due care as taking all measures a reasonably prudent patentee would take given circumstances.
propositions.quote: In the Decision, the Commissioner refers to the standard of due care as being “whether the patentee took all measures that a reasonably prudent patentee would have taken, given the particular set of circumstances to avoid the failure – and despite taking those measures – the failure nevertheless occurred.”

propositions.text: The Commissioner cited section 27.03 of MOPOP and paragraph 166M of the WIPO Guidelines as authority for this standard.
propositions.quote: The Commissioner makes reference to section 27.03 of the MOPOP as authority for this view, which recites the same standard of due care, noting that regard must also be given to paragraph 166M of the WIPO, Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) Receiving Office Guidelines.

propositions.text: The standard involves considering what else could have been reasonably expected to avoid the failure, considering circumstances and customary diligence.
propositions.quote: As set out in section 27.03.06 of the MOPOP, the Commissioner is to consider whether anything else could have been reasonably expected to have been done to avoid the failure in view of the surrounding circumstances, as well as the customary diligence that a prudent party would have exercised in the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The standard of due care involves taking all measures a reasonably prudent patentee would, considering circumstances and customary diligence, as per MOPOP and WIPO guidelines.

propositions.text: Section 27.03.06 of MOPOP states the Commissioner considers what else could have been reasonably expected to avoid failure, considering circumstances and diligence.
propositions.quote: As set out in section 27.03.06 of the MOPOP, the Commissioner is to consider whether anything else could have been reasonably expected to have been done to avoid the failure in view of the surrounding circumstances, as well as the customary diligence that a prudent party would have exercised in the circumstances.

propositions.text: The section emphasizes that measures taken after the failure are not considered, and the focus is on what could have been reasonably expected to avoid failure.
propositions.quote: Measures taken by the patentee after the failure occurred will not be taken into consideration in making the determination.

propositions.text: The section also refers to considerations from the WIPO Guidelines, acknowledging no two cases are identical.
propositions.quote: In making this determination, the Patent Office will have regard to considerations that are taken into account by the International Bureau and Receiving Offices as described in paragraph 166M of the Receiving Office Guidelines, while acknowledging that no two cases have identical sets of facts or circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: Section 27.03.06 of MOPOP guides considering what could have been reasonably expected to avoid failure, excluding post-failure actions, referencing WIPO considerations.

propositions.text: Paragraph 166M(d) of the Guidelines discusses the duty of applicant and agent to act with due care in communication, especially during miscommunication.
propositions.quote: Paragraph 166M(d) states the following with respect to miscommunication between an applicant and their agent: (d) Miscommunication between the Applicant and the Agent Where the applicant appoints an agent, both the applicant and the agent must act with “due care” in their communication with each other.

propositions.text: The paragraph states that both parties should act with due care, instruct clearly, clarify doubts, advise on important matters, and find alternative communication methods if needed.
propositions.quote: A prudent applicant instructs the agent in a clear and timely manner to file the international application. A prudent agent acts upon instructions received from the applicant and clarifies with the applicant in case of doubt. A prudent agent advises the applicant of all important matters in relation to the timely filing of an international application and the consequences of a late filing in a clear manner. A prudent applicant or agent finds alternative ways to communicate with the other person if the usual communication channels fail.

propositions.text: If technical difficulties occur, both parties may have acted with due care if they demonstrate system reliability and unanticipated breakdowns.
propositions.quote: A prudent applicant or agent acts upon instructions received from the applicant and clarifies with the applicant in case of doubt. A prudent agent advises the applicant of all important matters in relation to the timely filing of an international application and the consequences of a late filing in a clear manner. A prudent applicant or agent finds alternative ways to communicate with the other person if the usual communication channels fail. Where the failure to timely file an international application was caused by technical difficulties (e.g. unexpected email delivery failure between the applicant and the agent), both the applicant and the agent may have acted with “due care” if they can demonstrate that the system had worked reliably in the past and that the breakdown could not have been anticipated by either party.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 166M(d) emphasizes that both applicant and agent must act with due care, communicate clearly, clarify doubts, and find alternatives if needed, especially during technical issues.

propositions.text: The applicant argues the Commissioner applied a higher standard than the one in MOPOP, citing two passages from the Decision.
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues that the Commissioner applied a higher standard than the one conveyed to the Applicant and set out in the MOPOP. He refers to two primary passages from the Decision to support his argument.

propositions.text: The applicant points to a statement that to establish due care, all possible actions would be expected, claiming it is a higher standard than all measures a reasonably prudent patentee would take.
propositions.quote: First, the Applicant refers to the statement in the Decision that to establish due care it was expected that “all possible actions” would be taken.

propositions.text: The court finds that this statement must be read in context and, when so read, aligns with the standard of all measures a reasonably prudent patentee would take.
propositions.quote: As stated by the Commissioner, “to show due care, it is expected to take “all possible actions”, considering the circumstances of the case”. [emphasis added] The Commissioner refers consistently throughout the Decision to the reasonably prudent patentee as being the perspective from which such actions and the standard are to be considered.

propositions.text: The court concludes that the standard in the Decision is the same as in MOPOP, requiring all measures a reasonably prudent patentee would take in the circumstances.
propositions.quote: the reference to “all possible actions, considering the circumstances of the case” is the same standard as that stated in the MOPOP, which requires “all measures” that a reasonably prudent patentee would have taken in the circumstances.

propositions.text: The court does not find the applicant’s argument that the Commissioner’s reference to “all possible actions” implies a higher standard persuasive.
propositions.quote: it is clear that the reference to “all possible actions, considering the circumstances of the case” is the same standard as that stated in the MOPOP, which requires “all measures” that a reasonably prudent patentee would have taken in the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the standard in the Decision aligns with MOPOP, involving all measures a reasonably prudent patentee would take, not a higher standard.

propositions.text: The applicant points to a characterization in the Decision that the standard of due care doesn’t require all that was possible, suggesting a mischaracterization.
propositions.quote: The Applicant points to the Commissioner’s characterization of one of the arguments made by the Applicant in their Response, where the Commissioner states: “The standard of due care doesn’t require ‘all that was possible’, as suggested by the [Preliminary Decision].

propositions.text: The applicant claims this is a mischaracterization and reflects a higher standard that requires both reasonable and unreasonable measures.
propositions.quote: The Applicant asserts that this is a mischaracterization of their argument and is reflective of the higher standard that was applied - i.e., one that required both reasonable and unreasonable measures.

propositions.text: The court does not find this argument persuasive and states that the interpretation of the standard is consistent throughout the Decision.
propositions.quote: This section of the Decision is simply a summary of arguments made by the Applicant. It does not reflect the analysis applied by the Commissioner in the Decision. The interpretation of the standard is consistent throughout the Decision.

propositions.text: The court concludes that the standard is the same as in MOPOP, requiring all measures a reasonably prudent patentee would take, and the reference to “all possible actions” does not imply a higher standard.
propositions.quote: It is, in my view, the same standard as that published in section 27.03 of the MOPOP. It is one that requires all measures that a reasonably prudent patentee would have taken, given the set of circumstances related to the failure, to avoid the failure, and for the failure to have occurred despite having taken those measures. There is no suggestion that the Commissioner was looking to unreasonable measures and for the reasons I stated earlier, I do not view the Commissioner’s reference to “all possible actions, considering the circumstances of the case” to be inferring this.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the standard consistent with MOPOP, involving all measures a reasonably prudent patentee would take, not a higher or different standard.

propositions.text: The applicant claims the Commissioner’s characterization of the argument about the standard of due care is a mischaracterization.
propositions.quote: The Applicant points to the Commissioner’s characterization of one of the arguments made by the Applicant in their Response, where the Commissioner states: “The standard of due care doesn’t require ‘all that was possible’, as suggested by the [Preliminary Decision].

propositions.text: The applicant argues this mischaracterizes their argument and suggests the Commissioner applied a higher standard.
propositions.quote: The Applicant asserts that this is a mischaracterization of their argument and is reflective of the higher standard that was applied - i.e., one that required both reasonable and unreasonable measures.

propositions.text: The court finds that this section is a summary of arguments and does not reflect the analysis, and that the interpretation of the standard is consistent throughout.
propositions.quote: This section of the Decision is simply a summary of arguments made by the Applicant. It does not reflect the analysis applied by the Commissioner in the Decision. The interpretation of the standard is consistent throughout the Decision.

propositions.text: The court concludes that the standard is the same as in MOPOP, involving all measures a reasonably prudent patentee would take.
propositions.quote: It is, in my view, the same standard as that published in section 27.03 of the MOPOP. It is one that requires all measures that a reasonably prudent patentee would have taken, given the set of circumstances related to the failure, to avoid the failure, and for the failure to have occurred despite having taken those measures.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the standard consistent with MOPOP, involving all measures a reasonably prudent patentee would take, not a higher or different standard.

propositions.text: The court states that the interpretation of the standard is consistent throughout the Decision and involves all measures a reasonably prudent patentee would take.
propositions.quote: the interpretation of the standard is consistent throughout the Decision. It is, in my view, the same standard as that published in section 27.03 of the MOPOP. It is one that requires all measures that a reasonably prudent patentee would have taken in the circumstances.

propositions.text: The court does not find the applicant’s argument that the Commissioner’s reference to “all possible actions” implies a higher standard persuasive.
propositions.quote: There is no suggestion that the Commissioner was looking to unreasonable measures and for the reasons I stated earlier, I do not view the Commissioner’s reference to “all possible actions, considering the circumstances of the case” to be inferring this.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the standard consistent throughout the Decision, involving all measures a reasonably prudent patentee would take, not a higher standard.

propositions.text: The applicant argues that the example in paragraph 166M(d) of the Guidelines creates a legitimate expectation that if conditions are met, due care will be found.
propositions.quote: The applicant relies on the example cited in the passage from paragraph 166M(d) of the Guidelines (i.e., an unexpected email delivery failure between the applicant and the agent) to argue that where it is demonstrated that a system of email communication worked reliably in the past, and that the breakdown could not have been anticipated, due care should be found.

propositions.text: The applicant claims it was unreasonable and procedurally unfair to find otherwise, given the reference to section 27.03 of MOPOP and paragraph 166M(d).
propositions.quote: He argues that it was both unreasonable to find otherwise and procedurally unfair, as the reference to section 27.03 of the MOPOP and the example provided in paragraph 166M(d) created a legitimate expectation as to a standard that would be followed and if the conditions in the example were satisfied that due care would be found.

propositions.text: The court finds that neither of these arguments succeed, as the example is not a binding rule but a guideline.
propositions.quote: In my view, neither of these arguments can succeed.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant claims the example in paragraph 166M(d) creates a legitimate expectation of due care if conditions are met, but the court finds it is only a guideline.

propositions.text: The court considers this to be an issue of substantive review, not procedural fairness.
propositions.quote: First, I do not consider this to be an issue of procedural fairness. I agree with the Respondent that the same standard of due care that was identified in the Decision was set out in the Preliminary Decision.

propositions.text: The court states that the communication of the standard to the applicant does not create procedural fairness issues.
propositions.quote: The communication of the standard to the Applicant does not give rise to an issue of procedural fairness.

propositions.text: The court states that the issue is substantive review of the decision and the reasonableness of the application of the standard.
propositions.quote: Any issue with the application of the standard within the Decision relates to substantive review of the Decision and the standard of reasonableness.

paragraphs.summary: The court views the dispute over the standard as a substantive issue, not procedural fairness, and the standard was properly communicated.

propositions.text: The doctrine of legitimate expectations does not apply, as paragraph 166M(d) is a guideline, not a binding rule.
propositions.quote: It is also my view that the doctrine of legitimate expectations does not apply here. The example provided in paragraph 166M(d) does not create a clear and unqualified framework for the handling of reinstatement requests, and thus a legitimate expectation as to a procedural framework or anticipated result: Agraira v Canada, 2013 SCC 36 at paras 94-95; Congrégation des témoins de Jéhovah de St-Jérôme-Lafontaine v Lafontaine (Village), 2004 SCC 48.

propositions.text: The reference in paragraph 166M(d) is meant as a non-binding guideline, not a strict rule.
propositions.quote: Rather, the reference to paragraph 166M was intended to serve as a non-limiting guideline only.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 166M(d) is a non-binding guideline, not a strict rule, so legitimate expectations do not arise from it.

propositions.text: Paragraph 166M(d) uses the word “may” instead of “will”, indicating that technical difficulties do not automatically relieve parties of their duty to maintain effective communication.
propositions.quote: the example expressly uses the word “may” instead of “will” - “both the applicant and the agent may have acted with “due care” if they can demonstrate that the system had worked reliably in the past and that the breakdown could not have been anticipated by either party.”

propositions.text: Difficulties may justify failure to meet deadlines if system reliability is demonstrated, but do not relieve responsible parties from adopting other measures.
propositions.quote: While unexpected technical difficulties “may” justify the failure to meet a deadline in certain circumstances, I agree with the Respondent, such difficulties do not relieve the responsible parties from adopting other common sense measures to ensure that they maintain effective communication in the face of important deadlines.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 166M(d) states that technical difficulties may justify failure if system reliability is shown, but parties must still take other measures.

propositions.text: The Commissioner acknowledged the explanation of the Agent about the failure and efforts to remind the Applicant, but found them insufficient.
propositions.quote: In the Decision, the Commissioner acknowledged the explanation given by the Agent in their Response as to the circumstances around the failure to pay the maintenance fee, the efforts made by the Agent to remind the Applicant of the due date through email, and the unanticipated nature of the email correspondence going to the junk folder when correspondence to the same email address had been used reliably for years as the method of communication.

propositions.text: The Commissioner found that the efforts described were limited and insufficient to meet the standard of due care.
propositions.quote: However, the Commissioner found that the efforts made by the Agent and the Applicant as described in the Response, were limited and insufficient to meet the standard of due care in the circumstances at issue.

paragraphs.summary: The Commissioner found the efforts to address the email failure insufficient to meet the due care standard.

propositions.text: The Commissioner noted that the Response only focused on email efforts and did not describe other actions or systems to ensure effective communication.
propositions.quote: The Commissioner noted that the Response only focussed on email communication efforts to reach the Applicant and did not describe “any other action that was taken, or even considered, by the agent or the patentee, to ensure that communication channels remain[ed] effective and the Fees [we]re paid on time, despite the circumstances surrounding [the] case.”

propositions.text: There was no information on whether the Applicant had a system to monitor payment or manage email communication.
propositions.quote: Nor was there any information provided in the Response to address whether the Applicant had a system in place to monitor payment of the maintenance fee, or how email communication was managed to ensure it remained effective.

paragraphs.summary: The response lacked details on other actions or systems to ensure effective communication and timely payment.

propositions.text: The email failure involved multiple reminders over a year, critical for instructions on payment.
propositions.quote: In this instance, it is relevant that the email failure did not relate to a single piece of correspondence between the Agent and Applicant, but rather a string of email reminders and reporting emails that spanned over a year.

propositions.text: The communication was critical for the payment of the maintenance fee, which required instructions.
propositions.quote: The communication related to the payment of an annual maintenance fee upon which correspondence and instructions were required to complete payment and for which correspondence between the Applicant and Agent was critical.

paragraphs.summary: Multiple email reminders over a year were critical for instructions on paying the maintenance fee, and the email failure affected this process.

propositions.text: It was reasonable for the Commissioner to expect the patentee to have a system to ensure email effectiveness, given reliance on email for payment instructions.
propositions.quote: Similarly, in my view it was reasonable for the Commissioner to expect that a reasonably prudent patentee would have a system in place to make sure that their email was operating effectively if they were relying on this as the primary communication means to pay their maintenance fees.

propositions.text: Since the patentee retained responsibility for instructing the agent, they should exercise due care to ensure effective communication.
propositions.quote: Having retained this responsibility, it was reasonable for the Commissioner to find that it was incumbent on the Applicant to exercise due care to ensure that his email was properly receiving messages so that he could provide instructions to the Agent in a timely manner.

paragraphs.summary: The patentee was expected to have a system to ensure email effectiveness, as they relied on email for payment instructions and retained responsibility.

propositions.text: The email failure involved multiple reminders over a year, critical for instructions on payment.

propositions.text: It was reasonable for the Commissioner to consider steps to avoid communication failure and expect additional communication mechanisms.
propositions.quote: it was reasonable for the Commissioner to have looked at steps that could have avoided the communication failure and to have expected that the Agent would have additional communication mechanisms in place to make sure they could always correspond with the Applicant.

propositions.text: It was reasonable to expect that alternative measures would have been used to ensure patentee awareness of deadlines.
propositions.quote: it was likewise reasonable to have expected that in circumstances where numerous notices from the Agent had gone unanswered and where non-compliance could lead to expiry of patent rights that these alternative measures would have been used to ensure that the patentee was aware of the deadlines at issue.

propositions.text: The pattern of payment since 2012 supported the reasonableness of the expectations.
propositions.quote: Particularly as there had been a consistent pattern of payment since 2012.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it was reasonable for the Commissioner to consider steps to prevent communication failure and expect additional measures, given past payment patterns.
